Quarter ended December 31, 2021 $21,919,000]
findings.sourceCitation: §1.01, definition of "EBITDA" (concluding proviso following the fixed-quarter table)
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The SCHEDULE node in ir-definition:32c350f36f4d1860970bf978 captures the four fixed quarterly dollar amounts (cases[0]-[3]) and a formula-based defaultValue for all other periods, but contains no representation at all of the accompanying restriction that adjustments used to calculate those fixed historical amounts may not be used to adjust EBITDA for periods after December 31, 2021.
findings.verifierReasoning: The source contains two distinct operative instructions in this passage: (1) EBITDA for the four listed 2021 quarters is deemed to equal the fixed dollar figures, and (2) any adjustments (e.g., pro forma cost-savings/run-rate add-backs under clauses (a)(vii), (a)(viii), (a)(xviii)(b), which by their terms can have prospective effect for 12-18 months) that were baked into calculating those fixed historical figures may not be reused to adjust EBITDA in periods after 12/31/2021. This is an anti-double-counting/anti-carryover rule that is independently operative whenever a trailing-four-quarter EBITDA calculation spans the transition boundary (e.g., a period that includes Q4 2021 plus 2022 quarters computed via the formula). The proposed IR represents only the fixed-value substitution and drops the carryover restriction entirely, with no proviso, exception, or gating condition anywhere in the SCHEDULE node capturing it. A reviewer relying on the IR could incorrectly allow cost-savings/run-rate add-backs attributable to actions already reflected in the frozen 2021 baseline to be added back again in post-2021 periods, which the source explicitly forbids.

findings.sourceEvidence: “Applicable EBITDA” means, at any time, EBITDA for the Company and its Restricted Subsidiaries on a consolidated basis in accordance with GAAP for the period of four consecutive fiscal quarters...
findings.proposedIrEvidence: ir-definition:2f660825c4d06c8c85d1c437 is marked sufficiency: "COMPLETE", wrapping a DEFINED_TERM_REFERENCE to "EBITDA" in a DURING_PERIOD node, even though the sole substantive component it references - ir-definition:32c350f36f4d1860970bf978 (EBITDA) - is itself marked sufficiency: "PARTIAL" and contains numerous unresolved METRIC_REFERENCE placeholders (e.g., non-cash losses/expenses, Closing Date Transaction Expenses, the Combined Cap components, Disposed EBITDA, etc.) rather than fully resolved subexpressions.
findings.verifierReasoning: Applicable EBITDA has no independent computational content beyond "EBITDA for the trailing four quarters"; its entire numeric value is wholly derivative of the EBITDA definition. If sufficiency is meant to reflect whether a consumer can actually resolve/compute the term end-to-end, marking Applicable EBITDA COMPLETE while its only dependency is PARTIAL is a confident-but-potentially-misleading claim - exactly the scenario that deserves the most scrutiny. It is possible the compiler intends sufficiency to be scoped only to the local definition text (which was captured faithfully), in which case COMPLETE could be defensible; but absent an explicit convention disclosed in the IR, a downstream reviewer could reasonably be misled into believing Applicable EBITDA (used for leverage-ratio and Available Amount purposes) is fully computable when it is not.

findings.sourceEvidence: “Acquisition” means any transaction...by which any Loan Party or Restricted Subsidiary (a) acquires any going business or all or substantially all of the assets of any Person...
findings.proposedIrEvidence: dependsOnTerms: ["Equity Interests", "Restricted Subsidiary", "Effective Date"] - "Loan Party" is not listed despite being one of the two alternative acquiring-entity categories named in the operative text ("any Loan Party or Restricted Subsidiary").
findings.verifierReasoning: The entity-scope of who can consummate a qualifying Acquisition is defined disjunctively as a Loan Party OR a Restricted Subsidiary; omitting "Loan Party" from dependsOnTerms means the IR's declared dependency graph does not fully capture the entity scope of this definition. Because calculationExpression is null (this is a categorical, non-numeric definition) and no downstream rule in this IR currently consumes the term, the practical impact is limited, but it is a real, verifiable omission from the dependency list relative to the source text.

findings.sourceEvidence: "Applicable EBITDA" means, at any time, EBITDA for the Company and its Restricted Subsidiaries on a consolidated basis in accordance with GAAP for the period of four consecutive fiscal quarters... / "Acquired EBITDA" means, with respect to any Acquired Entity or Business for any period, the amount for such period of EBITDA of such Acquired Entity or Business...
findings.proposedIrEvidence: Both ir-definition:2f660825c4d06c8c85d1c437 (Applicable EBITDA) and ir-definition:ac176f9ef672747077231b94 (Acquired EBITDA) are marked sufficiency: "COMPLETE" and their calculationExpression is a METRIC_REFERENCE to metricName "EBITDA" with resolvedDefinitionId: null, even though the underlying "EBITDA" definition (ir-definition:32c350f36f4d1860970bf978) is itself marked sufficiency: "PARTIAL" with calculationExpression.kind="UNSUPPORTED" ("SUBTRACT operands do not type-check together").
findings.verifierReasoning: Applicable EBITDA and Acquired EBITDA are both defined purely in terms of the "EBITDA" component definition. The proposed IR's own EBITDA node is honestly disclosed as unresolved/unsupported (PARTIAL, UNSUPPORTED expression), and the dependent nodes never actually resolve their METRIC_REFERENCE back to that definition (resolvedDefinitionId is null). Marking Applicable EBITDA and Acquired EBITDA as COMPLETE is therefore an overconfident claim: neither can actually be computed until the EBITDA formula (with its extensive add-backs, the 20% Combined Cap, and the fixed quarterly override table for 2021) is resolved. A downstream consumer relying on the COMPLETE flag could reasonably (and wrongly) conclude these definitions are fully actionable, when in fact their sole computational input is admittedly broken. This is exactly the 'confident but wrong' pattern the verification process is meant to catch.

findings.sourceEvidence: "...provided that until the delivery to the Administrative Agent, pursuant to Section 5.01, of the Company’s consolidated financial information and Compliance Certificate for the Company’s first full fiscal quarter ending after the Effective Date, the “Applicable Rate” shall be the applicable rates per annum set forth below in Category 2... provided that at the option of the Administrative Agent or at the request of the Required Lenders, if the Borrowers fail to deliver the annual or quarterly consolidated financial statements required to be delivered by it pursuant to Section 5.01, the Total Net Leverage Ratio shall be deemed to be in Category 1 during the period from the expiration of the time for delivery thereof until such consolidated financial statements are delivered." ... "If at any time the Administrative Agent determines that the financial statements upon which the Applicable Rate was determined were incorrect... the Borrowers shall be required to retroactively pay any additional amount..."
findings.proposedIrEvidence: All four "Applicable Rate" IR nodes (ABR/Canadian Prime spread, Term Benchmark/CDOR/RFR spread, Commitment Fee Rate, Ticking Fee Rate) are modeled solely as a nested IF/COMPARE ladder keyed to the Total Net Leverage Ratio metric, with no branch, gate, or dependsOnTerms entry for: (a) the pre-first-quarter default to Category 2, (b) the deemed Category 1 override for delinquent financial statement delivery, or (c) the retroactive true-up obligation for inaccurate financials.
findings.verifierReasoning: The source text ties the Applicable Rate lookup to three independently operative overriding conditions that can supersede the plain TNLR-tier calculation: a default to Category 2 before the first full post-closing quarter's financials are delivered, a deemed-Category-1 penalty if the Borrowers become delinquent in delivering required financials, and a retroactive re-payment obligation if financial statements or compliance certificates used to set the rate are later found inaccurate. None of these are represented anywhere in the proposed IR's four Applicable Rate nodes, which compute the rate purely as a function of the current TNLR value. A hypothetical transaction where a Borrower is delinquent in delivering quarterly financials would, under the source text, be charged the Category 1 (highest) rate regardless of its actual computed TNLR, but the proposed IR would compute whatever rate the actual TNLR produces — potentially a materially lower rate. findings.verifierReasoning: The source text explicitly and repeatedly identifies which parties are bound by each obligation/prohibition: the Company is barred from designating the Administrative Agent as Auction Agent absent consent; the Company AND its Affiliates are separately and absolutely barred from acting as Auction Agent themselves; and the Borrowers (not Lenders, not the Administrative Agent) bear the retroactive payment obligation if financial statements are later found incorrect. None of this entity-scope information is captured anywhere in the IR despite each rule claiming COMPLETE sufficiency. A reviewer relying on the IR alone could not determine who is actually bound by any of these rules - e.g., whether an Affiliate of the Company (not the Company itself) attempting to act as Auction Agent would be a violation is knowable from the source ('neither the Company nor any of its Affiliates') but invisible from the IR. This is exactly the kind of entity/transaction scope omission the verification protocol calls out, and it is corroborated by the deterministic AMBIGUOUS signal flagging 4 distinct entity-scope terms (restricted subsidiaries, loan party, restricted subsidiary, borrower) with no corresponding entity-scope restriction recorded anywhere in the IR.

Neither the 'ABR' definition entry nor any of the four compiled rules contains a verifiable citation or content that maps to this restriction. If ir-rule:839fadccc906f4c35b1834c7 (the only rule with no citation at all, positioned first in the array, matching the ABR definition's position as the first entry in the document) is meant to represent it, the rule is an empty, contentless shell (no capacityExpression, no conditions, no entityScope, no description) that conveys none of the actual restriction, yet is marked COMPLETE. If it is not meant to represent it, the restriction is omitted from the IR altogether. Either way, a downstream compliance check relying on this IR could not correctly determine whether an ABR Loan denominated in a non-Dollar currency violates the Agreement.

findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR's "definitions" array contains only five entries (Alternate Base Rate, Adjusted Daily Simple SOFR, Adjusted Term SOFR Rate, Applicable Rate, Available Amount), all marked PARTIAL or UNSUPPORTED. Dozens of other terms actually defined in the operative Section 1.01 text supplied - including simple, fully-computable definitions such as Account Debtor, Administrative Agent, Affiliate, Agreed Currency, Alternative Currency, Anti-Corruption Laws, Auction Agent, and the entity-scope-bearing definition of "Acquisition" - have no corresponding entry at all, and there is no top-level sufficiency flag on the artifact disclosing that section coverage is partial.
findings.verifierReasoning:
Section 1.01 defines a very large number of terms, many trivially representable (e.g., 'Account Debtor' means any Person obligated on an Account; 'Agreed Currency' means dollars or any Alternative Currency), and at least one - 'Acquisition' - carries real operative/entity-scope content (restricting qualifying transactions to 'any Loan Party or Restricted Subsidiary', with two alternative tests in clauses (a) and (b)). The retrieved context bundle even shows this definition already decomposed into CHILD_RULE nodes for clauses (a) and (b), indicating the definition was recognized as structurally significant, yet the proposed IR contains no 'Acquisition' entry whatsoever, nor entries for the great majority of other defined terms in this section. The deterministic signals corroborate this: 8 enumerated sub-clauses with 0 compiled rules, 16 proviso/exception markers with 0 recorded conditions, and 4 distinct entity-scope terms (Loan Party, Restricted Subsidiary, Borrower, etc.) with no entity-scope restriction recorded anywhere in the IR. A downstream reviewer relying on this IR for the meaning of 'Acquisition' - which gates whether a transaction by, say, an Unrestricted Subsidiary or a non-Loan-Party affiliate qualifies as a Permitted Acquisition elsewhere in the agreement - would find no representation of that entity-scope limitation at all, and could reach a different conclusion about what counts as an 'Acquisition' than the real source text supports. Because the artifact does not disclose (at an aggregate level) that its definitional coverage of Section 1.01 is only a small, seemingly arbitrary subset, this omission is not offset by an honest disclosure comparable to the individual PARTIAL/UNSUPPORTED markings on the five terms that were included.

By contrast, the individual PARTIAL/UNSUPPORTED markings on Alternate Base Rate, Adjusted Daily Simple SOFR, Adjusted Term SOFR Rate, Applicable Rate, and Available Amount each candidly disclose why the compiler could not represent the relevant calculation (MAX/SUBTRACT type-check failures, multi-column grid limitations) and are not themselves treated as findings, consistent with the principle that an honest disclosure of a real limitation is not a semantic defect. The problem flagged here is the silent, undisclosed absence of the remaining bulk of the section's definitions, several of which are simple and clearly compilable, and at least one of which (Acquisition) carries independently operative entity-scope content that the deterministic AMBIGUOUS signals specifically call out as missing.'

findings.verifierReasoning: The source defines Acquired EBITDA not as a simple alias for the defined term 'EBITDA', but as a distinct metric computed by taking the EBITDA methodology and substituting every reference to 'the Company and its Restricted Subsidiaries' with 'such Acquired Entity or Business and its subsidiaries.' In other words, Acquired EBITDA is the acquired target's own stand-alone EBITDA calculated under the same formula, not the Company's consolidated EBITDA. The proposed IR instead models the calculationExpression as a bare DEFINED_TERM_REFERENCE to 'EBITDA' with no substitution/scoping mechanism at all - meaning as compiled, Acquired EBITDA would literally resolve to the Company's own consolidated EBITDA rather than the acquired business's EBITDA. This is a materially different economic result: e.g., if the Company's consolidated EBITDA is $50,000,000 and a small acquired business has its own EBITDA of $5,000,000, the correct Acquired EBITDA add-back (used elsewhere, e.g., in the EBITDA definition's clause (a)(xviii)(a) pro forma add-back for recently acquired entities) should be $5,000,000, but the proposed IR's formula would instead resolve to $50,000,000, a nine-fold overstatement. Although the definition is marked sufficiency PARTIAL rather than COMPLETE, the calculationExpression itself is not marked UNSUPPORTED - it makes an affirmative (and wrong) formula assertion, which is exactly the kind of confident-but-wrong representation this review is meant to catch, distinguishing it from an honest disclosure of a gap.

findings.verifierReasoning: The source text contains an important embedded proviso: the Section 6.12 financial covenant level used for pro forma calculations is determined WITHOUT giving effect to any Total Net Leverage Ratio Adjustment, EXCEPT when the calculation is being made to determine satisfaction of the conditions to a Permitted Acquisition (in which case the Adjustment IS given effect, consistent with the Permitted Acquisition definition clause (h)(i) which expressly says 'including any applicable Total Net Leverage Ratio Adjustment'). This carve-out/carve-back materially changes which leverage threshold applies depending on the purpose of the pro forma test - e.g., a company testing pro forma compliance generally uses the unadjusted level, but a company qualifying an Acquisition as a Permitted Acquisition uses the adjusted level. The proposed IR's r3 rule entirely omits this proviso from both its description and its (UNSUPPORTED) capacityExpression, and there is no exception entry capturing it either. A reviewer relying on this IR could conclude the wrong covenant level applies in a Permitted Acquisition qualification scenario, which is exactly the kind of transaction this section is designed to gate.

findings.verifierReasoning: The trigger for the entire pro forma adjustment mechanism explicitly applies when 'a Borrower or any Restricted Subsidiary' makes the relevant Acquisition/Disposition or consummates the relevant transaction - this is a disjunctive scope covering both entity types, not Borrower alone. The proposed IR's entityScope for this rule lists only 'BORROWER' and does not include Restricted Subsidiary, which materially narrows the scope of when this pro forma recalculation obligation is triggered. A transaction undertaken solely by a Restricted Subsidiary (which is the far more common scenario for operating-level acquisitions/dispositions) would, under the proposed IR's entityScope, appear outside the rule's stated scope even though the source text plainly includes it.

findings.proposedIrEvidence: description: "Self-executing designation operative under and in respect of any indenture or other agreement/instrument under which Subordinated Indebtedness is outstanding, whenever such Subordinated Indebtedness exists"; excerpt truncates at "...and words of similar import"
findings.verifierReasoning: The second operative sentence of §1.07 has two distinct operative components: (1) an enumerated designation of the Secured Obligations as 'senior indebtedness' and 'designated senior indebtedness' (and similar words), and (2) a separate, broader catch-all clause under which the Secured Obligations 'are further given all such other designations as shall be required under the terms of any such Subordinated Indebtedness' in order for Lenders to exercise payment-blockage or other senior-creditor remedies. This catch-all is independently operative: it extends the self-executing designation to labels or defined terms used in a particular subordinated debt instrument that may not be 'senior indebtedness' or 'designated senior indebtedness' verbatim (e.g., a custom defined term in a specific indenture). The proposed IR's second rule quotes only the enumerated-label portion of the sentence and its description/condition do not reference the sweep-up catch-all at all, so a reader relying on the IR could wrongly conclude that the designation is limited to the two enumerated labels, potentially missing that Lenders/Agent are entitled to whatever additional designation a specific Subordinated Indebtedness instrument requires. The rule is marked sufficiency PARTIAL, which is an honest general disclosure, but it does not specifically flag that this particular catch-all clause is the gap, so the omission is still worth surfacing on its own terms. I mark this UNCERTAIN rather than MATERIAL because this is largely boilerplate intended to preserve enforceability of payment-blockage rights vis-à-vis third-party subordinated noteholders, and is unlikely by itself to change a capacity, basket, or covenant-compliance conclusion under the Credit Agreement itself, but could matter in an actual subordination/enforcement dispute.

findings.sourceEvidence: "Without limiting the foregoing, the Secured Obligations are hereby designated ... as \"senior indebtedness\" and as \"designated senior indebtedness\" ... and are further given all such other designations as shall be required under the terms of any such Subordinated Indebtedness in order that the Lenders may have and exercise any payment blockage or other remedies..."
findings.verifierReasoning: The second sentence of §1.07 is a self-executing, present-tense contractual designation ('are hereby designated') that operates automatically upon execution/whenever Subordinated Indebtedness exists, independent of any act by a Loan Party. The opening phrase 'Without limiting the foregoing' expressly signals that this designation is additional to, and not contingent on performance of, the Borrower's separate covenant in the first sentence to 'take or cause ... to take all such actions as shall be necessary.' The proposed IR nonetheless represents this second rule with posture 'OBLIGATION' and entityScope ['LOAN_PARTY'], i.e., as an action-based duty imposed on the Loan Party. This mischaracterizes the legal effect: there is no Loan Party act or omission that could put this designation into or out of effect - it is automatically true by virtue of the Agreement's own language. A downstream compliance/monitoring consumer of the IR could wrongly treat this as an unperformed obligation capable of breach (e.g., requiring evidence the Loan Party 'did' something), when in fact the senior/designated-senior status attaches automatically and is not conditioned on Loan Party performance. This is a real difference in legal posture (self-operative declaration vs. an obligation owed by an entity) that could change a reviewer's compliance or enforcement analysis.
